title: Constructing receiver operating characteristics (ROCs) with experimental animals: Cautionary notes
research_question: This commentary critically examines the interpretation of linear Receiver Operating Characteristics (ROCs) obtained in rat odor-recognition tasks, questioning whether these ROCs reliably indicate selective impairment of recollection by hippocampal lesions or if they are artifacts of uncontrolled variables in the experimental procedure, particularly bias manipulation.

participants.description: Rats (control and hippocampal lesioned), humans (young, old, amnesic), pigeons, Patient Jon (human with bilateral hippocampal lesions).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Odor lists, odor pairs, words, pictures, faces used in various recognition memory tasks discussed.

measures.instrument: Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve (Hit Rate vs. False Alarm Rate)

findings.antecedent: Odor-recognition task in control rats (Sauvage et al. 2008)
findings.mechanism: Interpreted by Sauvage et al. (2008) as reflecting recollection based on the high-threshold/signal-detection model.
findings.quote: The shape of the ROC for control rats was linear

findings.antecedent: Odor-recognition task in rats with hippocampal lesions (Sauvage et al. 2008)
findings.mechanism: Interpreted by Sauvage et al. (2008) as reflecting familiarity based on the high-threshold/signal-detection model.
findings.quote: it was curvilinear for lesioned rats.

findings.mechanism: Based on interpretation of ROC shapes using high-threshold/signal-detection model.
Based on interpretation of ROC shapes using high-threshold/signal-detection model.

findings.antecedent: Odor-recognition procedure in control rats with long retention interval (30-75 min) (Fortin et al. 2004)
findings.mechanism: Fortin et al. (2004) suggested this occurred because familiarity faded more rapidly than recollection as the delay between study and test increased.
findings.quote: control rats produced linear ROCs following a long retention interval (30-75 min).

findings.mechanism: Weak memory conditions are generally associated with symmetrical curvilinear ROCs.
findings.quote: every other relevant study that has investigated the effect of retention interval on the shape of the ROC has found that a long retention interval yields a curvilinear function

findings.mechanism: As a general rule, weak memory conditions are associated with a symmetrical curvilinear ROC regardless of how memory strength is manipulated.
findings.quote: as a general rule, weak memory conditions are associated with a symmetrical curvilinear ROC

findings.antecedent: Associative recognition memory tasks (human literature, early reports)
findings.quote: A few early reports in the human literature suggested that ROCs based on associative recognition and related tasks might be linear

findings.antecedent: Associative recognition memory tasks (human literature, later review of 13 studies)
findings.quote: a later review of 13 associative recognition studies found them to be much better fit by a curvilinear function than by a linear function

findings.antecedent: Associative recognition memory tasks (human literature, 15 new ROCs from two laboratories)
findings.quote: 15 new associative recognition ROCs between them, and all have been curvilinear

findings.antecedent: Biasing manipulation in odor-recognition task (deep cups for New decision, shallow cups for Old decision) (Sauvage et al. 2008, Fortin et al. 2004)
findings.mechanism: The presence of a deep cup might reduce the willingness of the rat to carefully sample the test odor and instead to simply search for a more accessible reward.
findings.quote: the two conditions that used deep cups do appear to be associated with less accurate performance

findings.antecedent: Differential reward outcomes (general literature, e.g., Trapold 1970)
findings.mechanism: Known as the differential outcomes effect, where unique reward outcomes for different stimuli enhance performance.

findings.antecedent: Reward accessibility manipulation (e.g., making animal work harder) (Wilkie and Spetch 1978)
findings.mechanism: Manipulating reward accessibility affects accuracy, not just bias.
findings.quote: Still other studies show that manipulating the accessibility of reward (e.g., by making the animal work harder to obtain the reward) also affects accuracy

findings.antecedent: Overall amount of food reward (large vs. small) (Brown and White 2005)
findings.mechanism: May reflect altered motivation during the test.
findings.quote: When the overall reward amount was large, delayed matching accuracy was enhanced compared with when it was small

findings.antecedent: Patient Jon (human with bilateral hippocampal lesions) tested for memory of pictures (Bird et al. 2008)
findings.consequent: Shape of Old/New recognition Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC)
findings.mechanism: Bird et al. (2008) suggest this linear ROC probably reflects some idiosyncratic strategy for coping with weak memory, rather than pure recollection.
findings.quote: this patient (Patient Jon) produced the first linear Old/New ROC known to us in the extensive human literature on ROC analysis.

findings.antecedent: High-threshold/signal-detection model (Yonelinas 1994) applied to Patient Jon's linear ROC
findings.consequent: Interpretation of Patient Jon's memory process
findings.mechanism: According to the model, a linear ROC indicates purely recollection-based responding.
findings.quote: Patient Jon's ROC indicates purely recollection-based responding.

findings.antecedent: High-threshold/signal-detection model (Yonelinas 1994) applied to Patient Jon's linear ROC
findings.consequent: Conclusion about hippocampal lesions' effect on familiarity
findings.mechanism: Interpretation of Patient Jon's linear ROC would suggest hippocampal lesions selectively impair familiarity while preserving recollection, which is opposite to the conclusion from rat studies.
findings.quote: the results would suggest that hippocampal lesions selectively impair familiarity while preserving recollection (exactly the opposite of the conclusion reached by Fortin and colleagues and Sauvage and colleagues).

findings.antecedent: Differential reward magnitudes and different cup sizes (hypothetical experiment)
findings.mechanism: If accuracy were higher in shallow cup conditions or with large rewards, it would indicate these variables affect accuracy and should be held constant.
findings.quote: test directly the effects on accuracy of differential reward magnitudes and different cup sizes

mechanisms: Differential outcomes effect (association of unique reward outcomes with stimuli)
Idiosyncratic strategy for coping with weak memory
moderators: Signal presentation probability (proposed alternative bias manipulation)
implementation_implications: ROC data should be generated by an alternate method that does not involve differential difficulty and differential amounts of reward.
One could use identical reward outcomes for correct Old and New decisions, but manipulate bias by varying signal-presentation probability across test conditions.
Researchers should directly test the effects on accuracy of differential reward magnitudes and different cup sizes within the context of the odor-recognition procedure.
If accuracy is found to be higher with shallow cups, the size of food cups should be held constant across biasing conditions when constructing ROCs.
If accuracy is found to be higher with larger overall reward amounts, the overall reward for correct and incorrect responses should be held constant across biasing conditions when constructing ROCs.
limitations: It is difficult to determine whether performance is influenced only by memory (modulated by bias) or by changes in motivation, attention, or other non-memory factors.
Whether the specific biasing procedure used in the odor-recognition task maintains constant accuracy across conditions is unknown and has not been tested.
If accuracy varies across biasing conditions, interpreting the shape of the ROC becomes complicated.
It is not safe to assume that no uncontrolled effects occurred in the novel odor-recognition procedure, especially given its rare result of linear ROCs.
The extreme rarity of linear ROCs in recognition memory research raises questions about why the odor-recognition procedure yielded this pattern.

The rare linear ROCs produced by the odor-recognition procedure may be an artifact reflecting the influence of uncontrolled variables on accuracy, similar to effects known in other recognition memory procedures.

The idea that ROCs from the odor-recognition procedure imply selective impairment of recollection by hippocampal lesions should be viewed with caution until issues regarding uncontrolled variables are carefully investigated.
